newsitem.title: GERMANY: German union chief says jobs summit unlikely.
newsitem.headline: German union chief says jobs summit unlikely.

text.p: Germany's top trade union official said on Thursday that summit talks between unions, the government and employers to solve Germany's jobless problem were unlikely before a change in government policies.

Speaking in Duesseldorf, Dieter Schulte, chairman of the German Federation of Trade Unions (DGB) said the Bonn government "lacked the courage" to acknowledge the failure of policies that have led to rising unemployment.

He said that a previously-stated government goal of halving the nation's jobless total by 2000 must be met and that measures proposed by the DGB such as overtime reduction and job-sharing would allow it to be achieved.
Schulte's unwillingness to begin talks with the Bonn government were a rebuke for German Chancellor Helmut Kohl who had earlier said he was ready "day and night" to hold such discussions.

Kohl, speaking in Bonn after Germany's Federal Labour Office had released data showing a post-war seasonally-adjusted unemployment record of 4.16 million, said that fighting joblessness was his "most important domestic policy challenge".
He said he was ready for top-level discussions on job creation as long as all sides came to the discussions without making preconditions for the talks.
But the DGB has insisted that it would only participate in talks with the government and employers if the promises included in last year's failed "Alliance for Jobs" initiative were fulfilled.
Such promises included pledges by employers to create conditions for a reduction in overtime work and greater job-sharing, thus bringing more people into work.
In return, the trade unions were ready to accept moderate wage rises that would offer employers a degree of cost stability.

The Alliance for Jobs failed when the unions accused the government of betrayal in targeting labour-related and social costs in a tough austerity package of savings that it eventually introduced last September.
